Nicolas Burr, CEO, Grupo CAP

Tommee Larochelle, Managing Partner, L3 Process Development

Brad Fravel, Executive Director LINK, The Center for Advancing Partnerships, Virginia Tech

Pilot Plant Highlights

Aclara's separation pilot plant is now commissioned and operational.

Process designed to produce separated Dy, Tb and NdPr.

Fully staffed and prepared for continuous 24/7 operations since April.

Operational data already being generated to support development of an AI-driven digital twin, with progress advancing rapidly.

Dedicated team of Virginia Tech PhD researchers actively engaged in process optimization and advanced technical analysis.

The facility is expected to produce its first separated light rare earth oxides (NdPr) in May 2026 and heavy rare earth oxides (Dy and Tb) in August 2026.

Objectives of the pilot plant

The pilot plant will play a key role in advancing Aclara's U.S. industrial strategy by:

Validating Aclara's proprietary rare earth separation technology with feedstock from its ionic clay deposits in Brazil and Chile

Generating operational data to support the engineering, ramp-up, and optimization of the Company's commercial separation facility

Developing an AI-driven digital twin of the separation process in collaboration with Argonne National Laboratory; and

Training our workforce in rare earth separation and advanced hydrometallurgical processes

Integration with Aclara's planned Louisiana commercial facility

The Virginia Tech pilot plant is a critical step towards the development of Aclara's planned rare earth separation plant in Louisiana, which is expected to become the first facility in the United States capable of producing significant volumes of heavy rare earth oxides integrated with ionic clay deposits.

Aclara has selected a site at the Port of Vinton, Louisiana, for the development of this industrial facility, which is designed to produce high-purity Dysprosium, Terbium, Neodymium, and Praseodymium oxides used in permanent magnets and advanced technologies.

Key aspects of the Louisiana project include:

Engineering: Aclara has retained Hatch Ltd. to advance the engineering of the project and coordinate the integration with the Company's upstream mining operations.

Capital investment: Approximately US$277 million is expected to be invested to develop the commercial separation facility.

Permitting and incentives: The project is being developed in collaboration with the State of Louisiana, which is supporting the investment through $46.4 million in tax incentives and grants.

Production timeline: Subject to financing and project development milestones, the Company is targeting the start of operations for the Louisiana facility by mid-2028.

About Aclara

Aclara Resources Inc. (TSX: ARA), a Toronto Stock Exchange listed company, is focused on building a vertically integrated supply chain for rare earths alloys used in permanent magnets. This strategy is supported by Aclara's development of rare earth mineral resources hosted in ionic clay deposits, which contain high concentrations of the scarce heavy rare earths, providing the Company with a long-term, reliable source of these critical materials. The Company's rare earth mineral resource development projects include the Carina Project in the State of Goiás, Brazil as its flagship project and the Penco Module in the Biobío Region of Chile. Both projects feature Aclara's patented technology named Circular Mineral Harvesting, which offers a sustainable and energy-efficient extraction process for rare earths from ionic clay deposits. The Circular Mineral Harvesting process has been designed to minimize the water consumption and overall environmental impact through recycling and circular economy principles. Through its wholly-owned subsidiary, Aclara Technologies Inc., the Company is further enhancing its product value by developing a rare earths separation plant in the United States. This facility will process mixed rare earth carbonates sourced from Aclara's mineral resource projects, separating them into pure individual rare earth oxides. Additionally, Aclara through a joint venture with CAP, is advancing its alloy-making capabilities to convert these refined oxides into the alloys needed for fabricating permanent magnets. This joint venture leverages CAP's extensive expertise in metal refining and special ferro-alloyed steels. Beyond the Carina Project and the Penco Module, Aclara is committed to expanding its mineral resource portfolio by exploring greenfield opportunities and further developing projects within its existing concessions in Brazil, Chile, and Peru, aiming to increase future production of heavy rare earths.

This news release contains "forward-looking information" within the meaning of applicable securities legislation, which reflects the Company's current expectations regarding future events, including statements with regard to the anticipated validation and optimization of the Company's proprietary rare earth separation technology; the generation of operational data to support the engineering of a future industrial-scale plant in the United States; the expected production capacity, operational campaigns and performance objectives of the pilot-plant; the Company's ability to produce rare earth metals oxides in the pilot plant; the development and optimization of metallurgical processes and digital process models; the proposed industrial development of the industrial separation facility in Louisiana; the expected supply of high-purity mixed rare earth carbonates from the Company's ionic clay deposits in Brazil and Chile; the Company's vertical integration strategy across the rare earth value chain; and the timing of having a separation project ready for construction. Both projects feature Aclara's patented technology named Circular Mineral Harvesting, which offers a sustainable and energy-efficient extraction process for rare earths from ionic clay deposits. The Circular Mineral Harvesting process has been designed to minimize the water consumption and overall environmental impact through recycling and circular economy principles. Through its wholly-owned subsidiary, Aclara Technologies Inc., the Company is further enhancing its product value by developing a rare earths separation plant in the United States. This facility will process mixed rare earth carbonates sourced from Aclara's mineral resource projects, separating them into pure individual rare earth oxides. Additionally, Aclara through a joint venture with CAP, is advancing its alloy-making capabilities to convert these refined oxides into the alloys needed for fabricating permanent magnets. This joint venture leverages CAP's extensive expertise in metal refining and special ferro-alloyed steels. title: Tariff pressures cut through Michigan retail, driving price bumps and product shifts
authors: Crain's Detroit Business, www.facebook.com, Jay Davis
description:
Tariffs and the uncertainty surrounding them are taking a toll on small business owners across the state.
Higher wholesale prices are only part of the pressure Michigan small business owners are facing.
Around 62% of business owners surveyed by the MRA noted impacts to operational expenses.
“We’re not a grocery environment buying pallets of wine,” Vance said.
“We could shift entirely to domestic wines,” Vance said.
text:
Tariffs and the uncertainty surrounding them are taking a toll on small business owners across the state.

That's according to the results of a new survey from the Michigan Retailers Association, which found that nearly three-quarters of retailers queried say they’re experiencing negative impacts from tariffs since April.

Around 56.1% of the business owners surveyed said uncertainty surrounding tariffs has also affected their businesses, separate from the direct financial impact of the tariffs.

The survey of 66 MRA member business owners was conducted after the U.S. Supreme Court on Feb. 20 struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs. The MRA used the same methodology as a spring 2025 survey conducted after Trump announced a new tariffs plan on April 2. The February survey has a margin of error of about 10%, according to MRA Vice President of Communications Vic Veda.

For many retailers, rising inventory costs are the most immediate effect.

At Detroit-based Marrow Hospitality Group, Wine Buyer Bobby Vance said the impact of tariffs became noticeable in late 2025 and has intensified in recent months.

“We really started to see it in the last couple of quarters of 2025—definitely now, even more,” Vance told Crain’s. “What initially were small increases, maybe 50 cents a bottle, we’re now seeing wines that have gone up $3, $4, even $6 a bottle.”

Vance oversees wine purchasing for The Royce Detroit and all three Marrow locations in metro Detroit. He said overall wine costs have risen roughly 20%, driven largely by tariffs on imported goods. Vance uses several smaller global producers, with a heavy concentration in European wines, along with wines from South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina and Chile.

Tariffs have pushed up the price of imported goods, the survey found. Higher wholesale prices are only part of the pressure Michigan small business owners are facing.

Initially, Vance said, smaller producers and importers absorbed much of the tariffs burden to shield retailers and restaurants. That strategy, however, proved unsustainable, he said.

“As the tariffs have continued, that cost has gotten increasingly pushed to the last chain in the purchasing string,” he said.

Around 62% of business owners surveyed by the MRA noted impacts to operational expenses. About 51.5% said tariffs have disrupted future planning and 48.5% said sales volumes have been affected. Retailers also reported product disruptions tied to tariff costs.

The pressures from the tariffs are leading to full operational changes in some cases, according to the survey.

More than 83% of the retailers said they have adjusted their business strategies in response to the tariffs while about 62% reported raising prices on items. Around 29% said they have sought new inventory sources or suppliers, and 24% have delayed, modified or canceled planned projects. Only 16.7% of respondents said they have made no changes to their business strategies because of tariffs.

At The Royce, at 76 W. Adams Ave., Vance said the approach has been more nuanced. Rather than dramatically raising prices, the wine bar has shifted its selection to maintain its value-driven approach.

“We’ve always focused on wines $30 and under,” he said. “What that means now is we move to different wines at that price point. A wine that used to be $25 might now be $29 or $30.”

That strategy signals a big point of tension for small businesses, Vance said: balancing customer expectations with shrinking margins. While Marrow has largely maintained its markup structure, Vance said, some price increases inevitably reach customers.

“If a bottle costs us $12 and it goes to $16, we have to pass that on because the margins are so small,” he said.

Customer reaction to the price increases have been mixed but understanding, Vance said.

“They know what’s happening and that we don’t have a choice,” Vance said. “But they’re frustrated. People have favorites, and now they either pay more or stop buying them.”

For businesses like Marrow, scale adds another disadvantage, according to Vance.

“We’re not a grocery environment buying pallets of wine,” Vance said. “We’re buying in small quantities, so we don’t have the same leverage with importers and distributors.”

Despite the financial strain, Vance said tariffs have not yet affected staffing levels at the Marrow properties, but continued pressure could force deeper operational changes across the industry.

Another local business, Auburn Hills-based Whisker, has found itself in a relatively insulated position.

The manufacturer of the Litter-Robot self-cleaning cat litter box has largely avoided the issues caused by tariffs because of a longstanding strategy of designing and assembling its products in the United States, President and CEO Jacob Zuppke told Crain’s in an email.

Whisker has built its operating model around domestic production since it was founded more than 25 years ago by Brad Baxter in metro Detroit. What began as a practical decision has evolved into a competitive advantage, Zuppke said, particularly as tariffs have driven up costs for companies reliant on overseas manufacturing. Whisker imports some components of its machines, but the majority of the design, assembly and final quality control takes place in the U.S., he said.

The MRA report shows tariffs are affecting a large sector of a variety of industries, President and CEO Bill Hallan said in a statement to Crain’s.

“It’s clear that tariffs are negatively impacting the majority of Michigan’s retail industry,” Hallan said. “While a few sectors of our industry have seen benefits, like thrift shops and stores selling local produce and handmade goods, even those businesses experience strain with the uncertainty around tariffs and their impacts to consumer behavior.”

Vance said that uncertainty presents a problem he hopes Marrow and other businesses don’t have to address much longer.

“We could shift entirely to domestic wines,” Vance said. “But that would be a complete philosophical change for us. No business wants to be forced into that kind of decision because of policy.”

Zuppke said the current environment shows the value of domestic manufacturing and could push more companies to reconsider their supply chain.

“It’s not just about pride in being made in the USA,” he said. “It’s about ensuring consistency, quality and the ability to adapt quickly in a changing environment.”

text:
DETROIT LAKES — The clank and groan of an excavator lifting boulders filled the air the morning of March 9 as crews worked at the base of the historic, eight-spillway Bucks Mill Dam , where the Pelican River flows from Mill Pond into Buck Lake. Water poured around the machine’s tracks as it moved through the channel.

The dam has served as a key feature in the area’s water system for more than 150 years, according to the Pelican River Watershed District . A modification project began the week of Feb. 16, following extensive planning, hydraulic modeling and environmental review.

The DNR has secured up to $3.9 million for the project, part of its Reconnect the Red initiative to restore fish passage across the Red River Basin. Bucks Mill is one of the final barriers limiting access for species such as lake sturgeon and other native fish.

In recent weeks, some residents have expressed concern on social media that the dam is being removed, that Mill Pond could be drained or that a longtime fishing spot could disappear. But project engineer Garrett Monson of Moore Engineering, Inc. said the work is a modification, not a removal, designed to restore river function while maintaining lake levels and recreation.

“This has been a site that’s been in discussion for a long time, with myriad options and alternatives explored, so it makes sense that there might be some confusion or lack of clarity about what is or is not happening, because a lot has been said,” Monson said.

Monson said Bucks Mill has long been used as a case study for dam redesign, producing a range of concepts over time. The current project will replace the dam’s single drop with a series of rock “steps,” allowing fish to move upstream while improving sediment flow and channel stability.

The concrete structure that controls water levels will remain. Crews are removing the upper portions of the dam, including the walkway and railings, and installing a rock riffle system over and downstream of the existing spillway.

“Removing the dam was identified as a non-starter; not only would that have major implications on recreation in the area, it would also have major impacts on all the water resources, including lakes and wetlands, and all the habitat around and in those lakes and wetlands upstream of the dam,” Monson said.

Crews are laying smaller stone as a base, then placing 4- to 6-foot boulders across the channel to form low, curving weirs. Instead of a single, roughly 10-foot drop, the river will descend in steps of about 6 to 8 inches, creating a series of pools and shallow chutes.

Box culverts under the township road will be replaced with longer culverts, aligned more closely with the river. Additional culverts will allow water to spread across the floodplain, and the road will be raised so it no longer overtops with water during a 100-year flood.

Substantial completion is expected by October, with the contractor aiming to finish most visible work by mid- to late summer. Final vegetation and permitting work will continue into next year.

A primary goal of the project is to restore ecological function. The existing dam blocks fish movement and traps sediment — issues the riffle design is intended to address.

“The whole point of those riffles is to enable fish passage, and that’s to encourage habitat,” Monson said. “And it’s not just fish, it’s also macro invertebrates, and it’s good for vegetation too.”

The stepped design allows the river to drop gradually, with deeper pools and narrower chutes that keep water speeds within a range fish can navigate.

“Think of it as walking upstairs instead of trying to jump a wall,” Monson said. “So giving them a little step each part of the way, and then with the layout of those weirs, giving little areas to rest. They’ll have more narrow areas where they can jump up to the next level and work their way upstream.”

Restoring passage is especially important for lake sturgeon and other native species that historically migrated upstream to spawn. It also benefits mussels and aquatic insects.

“We’re bringing about restoration of the ecosystem that was in place prior to the dam being constructed, and so that’s going to have an ecological boost to the upstream waters,” Monson said.

The project also restores sediment movement — the sand, gravel and organic material that naturally flows downstream.

“Healthy rivers move, right? And they move because they are moving sediment,” Monson said. “It can be damaging to completely stop sediment transport. So it’s beneficial to design our systems so that we are allowing natural sediment transport to continue.”

Maintaining lake levels is a central requirement. Monson said the design was tested across a range of flow conditions to ensure water elevations remain consistent. Through hydraulic modeling, Monson said engineers kept a close eye on velocity ranges and the potential to change lake levels.

“Our final design is one that meets the needs of all those different categories where we’re not altering lake levels, and we are giving the fish what they need in order to get upstream while providing a safe and stable environment with no additional flood damage,” he said.

Construction is being completed with the river largely flowing through the site, with only temporary diversions in limited areas.

When complete, the site will take on a more natural appearance, with vegetation returning along the banks and between the rocks as the channel settles.

“What we’ve seen throughout the state when these projects occur is that these features often become community hot spots. Not only are they cool to see, but they’re a fun place to go enjoy,” Monson said.

Fishing is expected to remain strong and improve as habitat responds, he added, also explaining that Becker County is planning on developing a small park on the south side, with parking and trail access, and some boulders will be placed to provide fishing access.

text:
Louisiana will spend $1.54 billion on coastal projects over the next fiscal year under a plan approved Wednesday that solidifies a controversial shift away from large-scale river diversions, a major change in strategy pursued by Gov. Jeff Landry's administration.

The plan approved unanimously by the board of the state's Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority now goes to the state Legislature. Lawmakers must give it an up-or-down vote, with no ability to change individual projects, and it is typically overwhelmingly approved.

It lays out project spending for fiscal year 2027, which begins in July, and is separate from the CPRA's operational budget. Funding for projects comes from a combination of state and federal money, along with proceeds related to fines and settlements from the 2010 BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

This year's plan also includes $28 million from settlements with energy companies sued by Louisiana parishes over pollution and damage to the coastline. Most of that money is allocated for coastal restoration and shoreline protection efforts in Cameron Parish, in the state's far southwest.

The coastal authority's projects range from levee building to marsh creation and ecosystem restoration, with the aim of protecting the state from intensifying storms while addressing Louisiana's land loss crisis to as great an extent as possible. The state has lost around 2,000 square miles of land over the past century, about the size of Delaware, and sea level rise is projected to worsen the problem.

The authority's mission has traditionally received broad support from across the political spectrum, though debate over two large-scale river diversions aimed at restoring lost wetlands in recent years proved to be a high-profile exception.

Landry's administration has abandoned those plans in favor of a strategy that prioritizes restoring eroding barrier islands and rebuilding "land bridges" along vulnerable areas of Louisiana's coastline, though actual construction on much of that approach remains far off.

The change has been lauded by commercial fishermen and their parish leaders who strongly opposed the diversions, but harshly criticized by a range of scientists and coastal advocates who saw them as key to a broader strategy of salvaging parts of the coastline.

'Really moving forward'

But while debate over the now-canceled Mid-Barataria and Mid-Breton Sediment Diversions has been front and center, the new annual plan includes a total of 143 active projects across the state's coast. Of the $1.54 billion in total spending, proceeds linked to the BP spill account for about 27%, or $416 million.

"I think it is a reflection of the continued work that CPRA has been investing in for the past decade," said Michael Hare, executive director of the coastal authority. "And I think it's unfortunate that a lot of people focus on 'a project' in 'a place,' and then forget to recognize the 143 active projects across the entire coast."

CPRA Chairman Gordon Dove said "this is really moving forward, from pump stations to the levee systems, to coastal restoration, to marsh recreation, to land bridges to barrier islands..."

The plan approved by the board represents an increase over the $1.27 billion draft initially presented in December. That is due to the addition of coastal settlement dollars as well as a handful of projects being accelerated sooner than anticipated, said Hare.

Larger projects include continued work on the Morganza to the Gulf levee system for Terrebonne and Lafourche parishes as well as the West Shore Lake Pontchartrain levee system for St. Charles, St. John the Baptist and St. James parishes. It also includes funding toward restoring the disappearing Chandeleur Islands, among a long list of other projects.

Some coastal advocates noted the benefits that will occur from the annual plan, but lamented the diversions' cancelations and pressed the Landry administration to provide details of workable, large-scale alternatives.

"Many of the investments in this year’s annual plan will help sustain communities, wildlife habitat and a working coast economy, and we are encouraged to see them move forward," Restore the Mississippi River Delta, a coalition of national and local coastal advocacy organizations, said in a statement.

"However, the plan still falls short of what Louisianans deserve — a vision that matches the scale of the challenge, meaningful efforts to reconnect the river and restore natural processes, and regional restoration projects that deliver real benefits well into the future."

'Meaningful projects'

The Coalition to Restore Coastal Louisiana, the state's oldest coastal advocacy group and which also supported the diversions, said the new plan "represents meaningful projects across our coast, from Cameron Parish to St. Bernard."

"We hope that the state continues to look for ways to leverage Louisiana's economic boom to form fruitful public-private partnerships and to make beneficial use of dredged material," said CRCL government affairs director Ethan Melancon.

The large-scale land bridges prioritized by the Landry administration would be built with dredged sediment in the Terrebonne, Barataria and Breton basins. Much of that could potentially be paid for with BP funding formerly set aside for the diversions, though significant work remains to evaluate the plans and gain approval from trustees overseeing the money.

Those favoring the diversions note that land-building projects using dredged material work better when infusions of sediment from the river maintain them. That's because such rebuilding projects eventually erode and subside like the rest of the coast.

But commercial shrimpers and oyster farmers forcefully opposed the diversions because the fresh water that would accompany them would have forced them to move or go out of business.

The cost of the Mid-Barataria diversion, at more than $3 billion, was also criticized by Landry, who argued it was too much to spend on one project alone. More than $600 million had already been spent on it before it was canceled.

Those favoring the project said it matched the scale of Louisiana's land-loss crisis and that the BP funds provided a unique opportunity to build it.
